name: midwife

attributes.attribute: a folkloric figure of healing and prophecy at the door of birth
had second sight to see fairies stealing children
went to the Otherworld to steal back stolen infants
usually returned from fairy kidnapping unharmed

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The midwife is a folkloric motif tied to birth and death. In the past the door of birth was often the door of death as well. The midwife was a powerful figure at that door. She was usually a woman with knowledge of healing herbs and medicine. Among the Celts she was also believed to have the gift of prophecy, a gift granted to midwives in many cultures. She saw in the birth the patterns that ran through the child's whole life. The midwife had a kind of second sight that let her see when fairies were stealing human children. A midwife on the way to a late-night birth might meet such fairies. At the mother's home she would find the child dead, taken by those she had met. Legend tells of midwives who went to the Otherworld to steal back such infants. Midwives, poets, musicians, babies, and lovers were the people most likely to be taken by the fairies. Their skill was useful to the Otherworld, whose fairy children were often born weak and in need of care. Unlike most stolen people, midwives were usually returned unharmed and lived healthy lives.

okr.objective: Document the midwife and her place in Celtic folklore.
